A phone buzzed a split second before every jackpot. 🎰

In 2014 a team working for a group in St. Petersburg filmed slot machines, sent the videos to Russia, and got back the exact moment to press spin. They kept wins small so casinos wouldn't notice — and made over $250,000 a week. The flaw was in the machine's random number generator itself, so the casinos couldn't patch it.

Sources: WIRED (2017), U.S. Department of Justice (2014). Reconstruction, US case.

In 2014 a team linked to St. Petersburg filmed slot machines, sent the clips to Russia and got back the exact moments to press spin. Wins stayed small so no casino noticed — over $250,000 a week per team. The weakness was inside the machines' pseudo-random number generator, so casinos couldn't simply patch it.

Sources:
- WIRED, 'Russians Engineer a Brilliant Slot Machine Cheat' (Feb 2017)
- U.S. Department of Justice, Eastern District of Missouri, U.S. v. Murat Bliev (2014–2015)
